\section[escampar]{escampar — to stop raining, to clear up}

\label{lesson:ES-C697-escampar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for humid, then the Spanish for the humidity.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: escampar}
\textbf{escampar} — \textquotedblleft{}to stop raining, to clear up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Esperamos en el bar hasta que escampó.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We waited in the bar until it stopped raining.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ya ha escampado} — it has stopped raining.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{escampar} is usually explained as \emph{es-} and \emph{campo} \textquotedblleft{}field\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{campus}: first to clear a field, then for the sky to clear.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{escampar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{escampar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{escampar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for humid, then the Spanish for the humidity, then say \emph{escampar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does escampar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To stop raining, to clear up\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el chubasco]{el chubasco — the shower (of rain)}

\label{lesson:ES-C697-chubasco}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the humidity, then the Spanish for to stop raining.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el chubasco}
\textbf{el chubasco} — \textquotedblleft{}the shower (of rain)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Por la tarde habrá chubascos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There will be showers in the afternoon.}
\end{quote}

A forecast word for a short heavy shower.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{chubasco} comes from Portuguese \emph{chuvasco}, built on \emph{chuva} \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from Latin \emph{pluvia}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the humidity, then the Spanish for to stop raining, then say \emph{el chubasco} again

\section[el aguacero]{el aguacero — the downpour}

\label{lesson:ES-C697-aguacero}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to stop raining, then the Spanish for the shower.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el aguacero}
\textbf{el aguacero} — \textquotedblleft{}the downpour\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
De repente cayó un aguacero.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Suddenly there was a downpour.}

Heavier than \emph{un chubasco}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aguacero} is built on \emph{agua} \textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which is inherited from Latin \emph{aqua}.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[la llovizna]{la llovizna — the drizzle}

\label{lesson:ES-C697-llovizna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the shower, then the Spanish for the downpour.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la llovizna}
\textbf{la llovizna} — \textquotedblleft{}the drizzle\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Con esta llovizna no hace falta paraguas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{You do not need an umbrella in this drizzle.}
\end{quote}

Light, fine rain.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{llovizna} is built on \emph{lloviznar} \textquotedblleft{}to drizzle\textquotedblright{}, which comes from \emph{llover} \textquotedblleft{}to rain\textquotedblright{}, Latin \emph{pluere} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[lloviznar]{lloviznar — to drizzle}

\label{lesson:ES-C697-lloviznar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the downpour, then the Spanish for the drizzle.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lloviznar}
\textbf{lloviznar} — \textquotedblleft{}to drizzle\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}

Like \emph{llover}, used in the third person.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lloviznar} is built on \emph{llover} \textquotedblleft{}to rain\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which is inherited from Latin \emph{pluere}.
